title: ChatBLAS
subtitle: The First AI-Generated and Portable BLAS Library

sections.achievement: A team of Oak Ridge National Laboratory researchers introduced ChatBLAS, the first AI-generated and multi-vendor portable basic linear algebra subroutines, or BLAS, library. BLAS libraries are the foundational math libraries of high performance computing. The work proved that large language model, or LLM, code generation combined with human fine-tuning efforts provides either competitive or better performance than the highly optimized vendor-specific BLAS libraries. This work was presented at the SC24 AI4S workshop.
sections.impact: ChatBLAS demonstrates how LLMs, a revolutionary AI technology, can elevate productivity in the development, management, and optimization of the complex, highly specialized, and demanding HPC software ecosystem. The research team continues to quantify the impact of LLMs on fundamental HPC software by leveraging the large industry investment while identifying performance and trustworthiness gaps.

notes.presentation: TALKING POINTS: Created in 2012 and stable since 2018, the Julia programming language has been successfully adopted by industry (e.g. JuliaHub) and academia. Created in 2012 and stable since 2018, the Julia programming language has been successfully adopted by industry (e.g. JuliaHub) and academia. Its scientific (Fortran) and data science (Python) syntax combined with a unified ecosystem and performance via just-in-time (JIT) via LLVM provide a unique value proposition to accelerate scientific discovery. Gaps, such as performance portable CPU/GPU libraries, still exist in the Julia industry and academic driven ecosystem. We developed the first and only CPU/GPU high-level metaprogramming performance-portable model for the high-productive and LLVM-based programming model Julia. We evaluated the performance on different of JACC on well-known HPC and scientific workloads, such as the Conjugate Gradient algorithm, Lattice-Boltzmann method for Computational Fluid Dynamics Simulations, AI Convolutions, Image Processing, among others. JACC provides performance portability with near-zero overhead with respect to vendor-specific solutions. JACC had a strong presence at our premier SC24 conference: A paper about JACC was presented in the WACCPD workshop. A paper presented in the XLOOP workshop about connecting DOE’s SNS and OLCF user science facilities at ORNL used Julia and JACC. The work targeting ASCR IRI was awarded the best paper at the facilities workshop. JACC was used at the first ever Julia for HPC SC24 Tutorial showcasing a diffusion-reaction Gray-Scott code for the hands-on portion running on DOE’s NERSC Perlmutter supercomputer. The research poster on JACC was a finalist for the conference's best poster award (top 6 of 120+ posters). The work was presented for the final round and it was mentioned at the main stage awards ceremony at SC24. JACC efforts were also presented at the Julia for HPC BoF session. Scientists using JACC can achieve performance portable code via parallel_for and parallel_reduce constructs while offloading to multiple vendor CPU and GPU back ends (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel) Performance portability is key for several codes as large scale, our work would enable more accessible HPC capabilities and rapid prototyping of new ideas. Julia continues to be adopted by scientists looking for a balance approach to performance and productive science. Early adoption include uses by CERFACS in France, and currently engaging with SciDAC fusion projects and IRI. This line of work on high-productivity programming languages will continue through the Fairbanks project as part of the ASCR Competitive Portfolios Program. AWARDS: Best Research Poster Finalist (top 6 out of 120+) at SC24 REPRODUCIBILITY:  The paper has appendices and a badge for reproducibility by the WACCPD workshop organizers. JACC is open-source and hosted at GitHub: https://github.com/JuliaORNL/JACC.jl BACKGROUND AND CONTEXT INFORMATION:  We present JACC (Julia for ACCelerators), the first high-level, and performance-portable model for the just-in-time and LLVM-based Julia language. JACC provides a unified and lightweight front end across different back ends available in Julia, enabling the same Julia code to run efficiently on many HPC CPU and GPU targets. We evaluated the performance of JACC for common HPC kernels as well as for the most computationally demanding kernels used in applications, HPCCG, a supercomputing benchmark test for sparse domains, and HARVEY, a blood flow simulator to assist in the diagnosis and treatment of patients suffering from vascular diseases. We carried out the performance analysis on the most advanced US DOE supercomputers: Aurora, Frontier, and Perlmutter. Overall, we show that JACC has a negligible overhead versus vendor-specific solutions, reporting GPU speedups with no extra cost to programmability.
